Among iOS 27’s many newly introduced features is a great change for anyone with multiple iPhones: you can now keep the same phone number on two iPhones via iPhone Handoff.

With iOS 27, Apple introduces substantial AI upgrades like Siri AI, plus exciting upcoming features for apps like Wallet, Messages, Notes, and also CarPlay and AirPods.

But the update also has a lot of smaller, more niche improvements.

One such addition is iPhone Handoff, which enables switching seamlessly between two iPhones using the same phone number.

Here’s how it works, per Apple:.

After iPhone Handoff is set up, one iPhone becomes the main iPhone and the other iPhone becomes the secondary iPhone that shares the number. Your main iPhone should be the one you use most often. Some carrier services, like Call Forwarding and Caller ID, and carrier account management can only be managed on your main iPhone. Contact your carrier for more details.

To move between your main iPhone and secondary iPhone, simply unlock the device that you want to start using — your phone number will automatically become active on that device. The message “Switched to this iPhone” will display at the top of your screen to confirm it’s now active. Your phone number will only be active on one iPhone at a time when using iPhone Handoff.

Most people will never need this feature. But if you’re someone who, for whatever reason, has separate devices that you want on the same number, iOS 27 has the solution.

Industry observers note that I feel like I’m exactly who this feature was made for. After years of running dual SIM, I now have a personal line on my Duo and work line on an 18 Pro. Going out with friends, family, etc, I’d love to bring one phone again while bringing both numbers with me, but keeping work system access to a specific, separate device. Only current problem is waiting for Verizon to activate the feature and then see if it actually works well.

If you’re trying to decide between an iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, perhaps iPhone Handoff is Apple’s subtle way of saying: “Why choose?”.

So far carrier support is limited (here’s the latest list), but Apple intends to expand iPhone Handoff to more carriers soon.

Do you have a need to use the same phone number on multiple iPhones? For what reason? Let us know in the comments.

Industry News: Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB Memory

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, lookAtMyQuant is a quantization compiler.
  • On Gemma 4 E2B, its GGUF has 12× lower KL than Q4_K_M at the same file size.
  • In a recent development, lookAtMyQuant 2 takes Qwen3.5-4B to 1.23 GB, 2.3 bits per weight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, lookAtMyQuant is a quantization compiler. It measures how much each stored piece of a model hurts the output when compressed. It then picks a code for each piece so the whole model fits a size budget with the least damage.

On Gemma 4 E2B, its GGUF has 12× lower KL than Q4_K_M at the same file size. The method and every result are on the site.

The code is under the MIT license.

In a recent development, lookAtMyQuant 2 takes Qwen3.5-4B to 1.23 GB, 2.3 bits per weight. The file solves 330 of 540 exact-answer math problems. Prism ML's Bonsai 2 Ternary 4B solves 328 at 1.20 GB, and the original solves 359. Its KL from the original on held-out text is 0.45 nats, against 0.59 for Bonsai.

Recent findings suggest that the recipe is post-training quantization with trellis codes, calibrated on the model's own worked math solutions with digit tokens weighted 10×, and with bits allocated per row by Fisher information. 4,000 steps of distillation follow, in which every layer is re-quantized once from the original weights. The page has the findings, the full recipe and its cost, about $34 of GPU time.

It has been revealed that the recipe's code is here, and the next section runs it. The 1.23 GB file itself is the lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb release, packed for the Apple Silicon runtime.

In a recent development, the same recipe takes Qwen3.8-27B from 53.7 GB to 7.2 GB, 2.1 bits per weight, calibrated and distilled on English prose and chat, code and math. The file solves 401 of the 540 math problems, as many as the original, and Unsloth's UD-IQ2_XXS GGUF of the same size solves 348. It also scores above that GGUF on HumanEval (73.8% against 67.1%), MMLU (78.8% against 75.0%) and GSM8K (94.5% against 92.7%).

Beside it sits a 4-bit DSpine drafter (1.02 GB, converted from tencent/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16 with runtime_mlx/convert_dspine.py and packed with pack_drafter.py), which roughly doubles decode speed on math and code on Apple silicon.

The same compiler and proximal fine-tuning (SQYFR), extended to a 26.4B physical / 5.4B active 3×-looped MoE (L6–17 looped 3× = 48 logical visits, 128 experts top-8), compresses thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini from 18.89 GB of text weights to 5.38 GB (1.63 bits/weight) and 8.87 GB (2.69 bits/weight) using 4 KB SRAM hashed block-vector trellis codes (ht2/ht3), row trellis codes (rtr1/rtr4), and a tr2 floor on the tail lm_head bucket (head.7).

Evaluated on the same BF16 teacher, openai/gsm8k (test[:200], greedy, reasoning_effort="none"), all 164 executable openai/openai_humaneval problems, 4 Vision VQA tests (with the untouched 637 MB BF16 vision tower), and 16+13-language TextMix windows:.

At 5.38 GB, Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-5.4GB outscores Unsloth's 9.14 GB UD-Q2_K_XL on both GSM8K and HumanEval at 41% smaller size (up from 76/200 and 24/164 untuned). At 8.87 GB, Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-8.9GB matches the BF16 original on GSM8K and cuts KL 2.34× on English/chat/code and 29.6% across all 13 languages below UD-Q2_K_XL. Both run directly through lamq and runtime_mlx with custom Apple Silicon Metal kernels, optionally paired with the 178.9 MB 4-bit DSpark drafter: on M5 Max, 5.4 GB decodes at 73.2 tok/s serial and 125.2 tok/s median (141.8 tok/s math, 129.0 tok/s reasoning, 121.4 tok/s code, 102.3 tok/s prose; 1,037 tok/s prefill at T=512, 5.83 GB active RAM), and 8.9 GB decodes at 63.1 tok/s serial and 101.3 tok/s median (133.9 tok/s reasoning, 118.9 tok/s math; 838 tok/s prefill at T=512, 9.32 GB active RAM).

On Apple silicon, install the runtime package directly (this installs mlx, mlx-lm, numpy, and huggingface-hub without the PyTorch compiler dependencies):.

From a local clone, pip install -e . installs the lamq command, or run python -m runtime_mlx without installing.

Sources indicate that command line. Pass either a local model folder or a Hugging Face repo ID:.

lamq generate reads stdin when -p is omitted, supports --raw, --system, --thinking, --temp, --mode linear|chat-fork|copy-wide, --no-adaptive, and --json. lamq info inspects a packed model's format and dimensions without loading weights.

It has been revealed that python integration. runtime_mlx.load returns an (model, tokenizer) pair compatible with mlx_lm.generate and mlx_lm.stream_generate (auto-detecting opgraph-packed-1 models such as Qwen3.5-4B / Qwen3.8-27B and lamq.json exports such as Gemma 4 E2B):.

For streaming, multi-turn chat, or speculative decoding through one interface, use Runtime:.

Sources indicate that install the dependencies and download the model and WikiText-2. The code reads SmolLM2-360M's config when it starts, so do this first.

Measure. This compresses one piece at a time, leaves the rest exact, and records the KL to the original model. The full set for this model, 2,312 measurements, took about 50 minutes on an L40S.

According to recent reports, allocate. This picks one code per piece, with the least summed KL inside the budget. It needs no GPU. This command uses the SmolLM2-360M measurements in this repository, with a budget of 3.044 bits per weight.

The blueprint it writes has the same widths as results/compiler/plans/sm_lin_3044.json.

Industry observers note that build and score. This quantizes the model to the initiative, one matrix at a time. It then reports perplexity and KL to the original on WikiText-2 test.

Sources indicate that our run of that blueprint is in results/batch/cc_sm_lin_3044.json. It reached perplexity 16.64 and KL 0.0926, against an original perplexity of 15.31. Add --layers 1 --calib 8 --eval 2 for a quick check that everything works.

According to recent reports, each step is a named job; python run_batch.py --list prints its command. The jobs need Qwen3.5-4B in models/Qwen3.5-4B on the volume and the text mix (modal run --detach modal_fetch.py --text). Every file they make goes to lm2/ on the volume.

lm2BuildSmoke, lm2FinetuneSmoke and lm2MathSmoke run the same code on two layers, 60 steps and 36 problems, in a few minutes each.

The row plan. lm2Build reads results/compiler/rows/q35_rowplan_1p2GB.json, which gives 1 to 4 bits to each of 1,520 row groups. row_allocation.py made it. Its build-control command builds and packs a control with a fixed split of rows, prepare-rows allocates rows inside the control's packed bytes with rowgroup_alloc.py, and build-rows builds under the plan and checks the packed size against it.

It has been revealed that the codebooks. The four e-means codebooks the build decodes with are in cache/codes/. --trellis-fit lloyd gives the earlier ones, and a blueprint made before the change keeps them unless the flag states otherwise.

Recent findings suggest that recent equal-byte recipe improvements. Two zero-byte additions are available in the compiler and fine-tuning scripts:.

According to recent reports, where these jobs differ from our run. Our GSM8K solutions were written earlier, with thinking always off. Our text KL on 13 sources used 52 windows picked from the text mix by a separate tool; --sources mix takes the mix's own evaluation windows, on which our file scores 0.44 where the page reports 0.45.

run_batch.py names every job, and modal_app.py runs them. modal_fetch.py downloads models and the text mix used for calibration and evaluation.

The runs behind the site used these machines, each with 8 CPU cores:.

Industry observers note that gguf_compiler.py makes looks out of llama.cpp's own tensor types, so the result runs in llama.cpp as it is. public_eval.py scores public quantizations the same way as our plans. Both run inside the image in modal_gguf.py, which builds llama.cpp with CUDA.

Sources indicate that quantize.py --export writes a blueprint in the format runtime_mlx/ reads. A plan with trellis codes also needs --trellis-rows 16,8, which runs each trellis path along a row of its matrix, so that decoding an entry reads only that row. On Apple silicon, pip install . installs mlx and mlx-lm; requirements.txt holds the PyTorch compiler dependencies.

On Gemma 4 E2B at 2.5 GB, the trellis initiative has 26% lower KL than the Lloyd–Max plan and decodes about 22% slower. runtime_mlx/test_trellis_gen.py and runtime_mlx/test_trellis.py check the trellis kernels against the matrices the quantizer built.

runtime_mlx/fast_q35.py decodes the packed 1.2 GB Qwen3.5-4B file one token at a time, straight from its trellis codes. runtime_mlx/drafter_q35.py adds speculative decoding. A small drafter proposes the seven tokens after the model's latest one in a single pass. The model then checks all eight positions in one pass over its coded weights (runtime_mlx/block_q35.py) and keeps the proposals that match its own choice, so the text is exactly its own greedy text.

On an M5 Max, over 30 held-out prompts of up to 256 tokens, generation with the drafter was 2.0 times as fast: 176 tokens a second against 88, timed in alternation in one process on 2026-11-11. A check kept 4.3 tokens on average. Over eight everyday prompts it was 1.5 times as fast. The gain follows how predictable the text is: 2.5 times on algebra, 2.0 on code, 1.2 on chat and 1.05 on a story, and one of the 30 held-out prompts ran slower with the drafter. The text matched plain greedy decoding on every prompt. These are speeds after the first token; reading the prompt takes about 0.1 s either way.

Two later changes are in this code. Each was measured against the version before it on 40 paired generations: proposing from the 96,033 most common tokens was 6.0% faster, and picking the winning token inside the packed product was 5.3% faster. Linear mode also enables self-calibrating adaptive fallback by default (adaptive=True; pass --no-adaptive to disable): when rolling acceptance drops below the measured break-even ratio of drafted-check latency to serial-step latency (accounting for cache flush and drafter context replay), it pauses drafting for short exact serial bursts and resumes once acceptance recovers, preserving bit-exact greedy parity while avoiding slowdowns on low-acceptance prose.

Sources indicate that the drafter is a DSpine model, trained with SpecForge from the published DFlash drafter for Qwen3.5-4B on the 1.2 GB file's own greedy answers. modal_drafter.py runs the training as one Modal job, and it cost $42. On 300 held-out prompts the trained drafter gets 4.65 tokens per check, against 4.30 for the stock DFlash drafter.

pack_drafter.py stores the drafter at 4 bits a weight in the build's own code, with no calibration data: 464 MB against 1.83 GB at 16 bits. On 60 held-out prompts the 4-bit drafter kept 4.35 tokens per check against 4.38, and the text was the same. drafter_q35.py loads either form and writes the packed one out dense as it loads. The 4-bit drafter is the lm2-drafter-4bit release. It runs beside the packed 1.2 GB file, the lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb release.

The benchmark defaults to linear verification. Use --mode chat-fork to try a second candidate at an ambiguous early position, or --mode copy-wide for known contiguous copies. Copy mode uses the source cursor and tunes the gate/up and down projections for 16-slot checks. Both modes verify all emitted tokens with the packed target. To benchmark the chat fork, run:.

For a copy benchmark, pass --mode copy-wide --heldout path/to/copy-prompts.json. The JSON entries carry source, prompt_len, and input_ids from the packed model's tokenizer.

The checks, and the packer for a drafter of your own:.

In a recent development, runtime_mlx/pack_dense.py writes the packed file from the fine-tuned build's dense weights, and runtime_mlx/modal_pack.py runs it on Modal. check_drafter.py compares the drafter in MLX with SpecForge's own model on reference blocks that drafter/reference.py writes.

Each test file runs on its own from the repository root, and all seven finish in under a minute.

Recent findings suggest that runtime_mlx/test_core.py checks the runtime against the quantizer's math. Run python runtime_mlx/make_ref.py first, which writes 1.6 GB of reference files.

In a recent development, runtime_mlx/test_fast_q35.py and runtime_mlx/test_block_q35.py check the Qwen3.5 kernels against NumPy products of independently unpacked codes, with no model. When LAMQ_Q35_PACKED names a packed file, the second also checks a block of tokens against decoding them one at a time. When LAMQ_Q38_PACKED names the packed Qwen3.8-27B file, it runs the same checks on a model whose output head is stored apart from its embedding.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Gran – Nov 21, 2026 at 9:45AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF ›.

The S&P 500 index (^GSPC -3.70%) includes the 500 largest publicly traded companies in America. Its name is often interchangeable with "the stock market" because the 500 large-cap stocks in this index make up about 80% of the total U.S. stock market capitalization.

So, when "the stock market" (as in the S&P 500) loses more than 10% of its value in a month, people get nervous. As of Nov. 20, since reaching its record high on Oct. 6, the S&P 500 is down about 11.6%.

The biggest driver of this recent stock market swoon is the same reason stocks have been delivering such strong results since 2022: the artificial intelligence (AI) industry. Big-spending AI hyperscalers and innovative AI frontier labs have been buoyed by investor enthusiasm for futuristic technology that promises to boost productivity and economic growth.

But to get to that bright future, these AI companies have been spending (and borrowing) hundreds of billions of dollars. Investors are starting to balk at the high price of AI. As a result of these AI fears, the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 index has fallen even further than the S&P 500. The tech sector benchmark is down about 20% since Oct. 6 -- heading into a bear market.

Industry observers note that it's understandable to feel nervous when the stock market is falling like this, but investors need to take heart, stay calm, and have confidence in the future. If you've been investing as long as I have (or longer), you've lived through worse than this.

Here's one move I'm making with my investments right now and one I'm avoiding.

It's easy to say and harder to do, but it's true: When stock prices are plummeting, that's when I try to just keep buying more stocks. A 10% stock market correction or a 20% (or worse) bear market is ironically the best time to buy stocks. It means stocks are "on sale.".

It has been revealed that so that's what I'm doing. I'm going to keep buying stocks in a diversified portfolio of low-cost index funds. My favorite U.S. index fund is the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF (VTI -3.52%) because it lets me own 3,511 U.S. stocks of all sizes and industries, not just the tech sector.

NYSEMKT · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

Additionally, times when the U.S. stock market is struggling can be good occasions to diversify with international stocks. I'm going to keep buying the Vanguard Total International Stock ETF (VXUS -3.27%) and its remarkably diversified portfolio of 8,874 stocks from dozens of other countries beyond the U.S. market.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

Eviedence indicates that corrections and bear markets are temporary. If you look at the long run of stock market history, the S&P 500 has always bounced back from even the biggest stock market crashes and economic crises.

Because I'm diversified with a portfolio of thousands of stocks from the U.S. and around the world, I believe that there's never a "bad time" to buy stocks. The stock market might keep falling for a while, even after I buy my next shares -- that's OK. I don't know which individual companies or industries will be the winners or losers -- that's fine, too. By owning these index funds, I'm betting on the stock market itself to sort out the winners for me.

Buying "all the stocks" this way lets me own a piece of the global economy’s long-term upside.

It's usually a bad idea for investors to sell stocks during a bear market. It's a little like selling a car or a house that's underwater on the loan -- it puts you in a disadvantaged position and locks in your losses.

(The only exception is if you have individual stock positions that you no longer believe in and want to sell at a loss for tax-loss harvesting purposes. That's a longer conversation to be had with a professional tax advisor.).

With a diversified portfolio of index funds that I'm holding for the long term, I'm not looking to sell anything right now. That's because I don't need the money out of my investment portfolio right now; I need it 20 or 30 years in the future. I don't need to liquidate my investment portfolio for cash. I don't need my stocks to go up today or tomorrow or next year. I need them to deliver long-term returns for the next 20 years or more.

Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • Recent findings suggest that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • It has been revealed that these ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

In a recent development, many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon declared his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

Recent findings suggest that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

It has been revealed that these ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

In a recent development, amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is vital because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

It has been revealed that I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

In a recent development, RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company revealed a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

In a recent development, but do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Recent findings suggest that such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

A Useful AI FuturePowerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s at the moment receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.Penny Gray PhotographyObjection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s right now receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

In a recent development, there’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

Recent findings suggest that but this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

In a recent development, we cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

Sources indicate that at the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s vital to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky rapidly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a fresh instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the tech giant’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

Sources indicate that these examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

According to recent reports, using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In a recent development, in the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

It has been revealed that the misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted looks for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

In a recent development, even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the organization judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

Industry observers note that this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

In a recent development, what’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

This article appears in the December 2026 print problem as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”.

Industry observers note that apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

It has been revealed that if you ask any Mac admin for a list of the software on their fleet, they’ll pull up their device management inventory and show you the apps they’ve deployed. Ask them what their developers installed with Homebrew last month, which VS Code extensions they are running, or what npm pulled into a project on Tuesday, and you’ll get a different response. That software was never procured by finance, never approved, and never inventoried. It’s also where a growing share of the risk lives in the AI era. Workbrew 2.0 treats that gap as a problem worth solving for IT teams.

In a recent development, about Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train consumers, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

In a recent development, device management is built around the software IT deploys. Apps from Apple Business Manager, apps preloaded via your device management vendors’ packages, packages you upload, and profiles you push out. That model solves the problem for native macOS apps. It doesn’t cover what happens when the Mac becomes the default developer machine. Developers install what they need with a single command in Terminal, and Homebrew alone has more than 16,000 packages. You then add millions of npm packages and hundreds of thousands of IDE extensions, and the list of software on a Mac that IT didn’t put there is longer than the list it did.

According to recent reports, that used to be a developer-only problem. It isn’t anymore, in the vibe-coding era. AI tools have turned marketers, analysts, and ops people into builders, and those builders install packages too.

Workbrew started as a management layer for Homebrew: an agent that reports what’s installed, flags known vulnerabilities, and lets IT push updates across the fleet. Version 2.0 expands the catalog to include npm packages, VS Code extensions, and macOS apps, all in a single inventory. The firm states it has patched more than 10 million vulnerabilities for customers since its launch, and it’s now ISO 27001-certified.

The part that is critical for everyone who isn’t a developer is the new Workbrew app, a native Mac app for finding, installing, and updating approved software. Workbrew calls it “the app store for your entire company.” Employees can browse what IT has approved, install it without opening Terminal, and request anything that isn’t on the list. IT approves or denies in the Workbrew Console, and if it’s a no, the employee gets an answer on why.

According to recent reports, the app comes from the Updatest team, which Workbrew acquired as part of this release. Updatest is the indie Mac app that keeps thousands of people’ software up to date, and it remains a separate product for individuals and families. For business customer, that experience is now the Workbrew app, and it’s included on every plan, including the free Team plan with no device or user limits.

With Workbrew, we finally have real visibility into what developers are using in Homebrew. Fleet-wide updates are effortless, and the team stays secure without being slowed down.

Chris Merrell, Director of IT, End User Services, Camping World.

Workbrew isn’t a device management tool and isn’t trying to be one. Your device management system deploys the Workbrew agent, and Workbrew handles software your device management system lacks visibility into. If your fleet consists entirely of office workers on managed apps, there’s nothing here for you. If you have developers, or you’ve noticed the marketing team installing things to run AI scripts, you have the problem whether you’ve discovered it or not.

It has been revealed that AI tools have changed how we think about app management, because apps get installed differently now. Workbrew 2.0 provides IT with a list of development tools on the Mac and gives employees a sanctioned way to get what they need.

Workbrew 2.0 is now available with a free Team initiative and no device or user limits.

According to recent reports, there’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

Industry observers note that for Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other vital parts of your digital life — organized.

Take a look at Proton’s Black Friday offers, starting at $1.99 per month.

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

In a recent development, unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

It has been revealed that proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

An alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

It has been revealed that if that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

It’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

Proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

When you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Industry observers note that pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

📖 Baca

5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1175 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that at the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities.
  • Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?
  • In a recent development, the capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that at the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities. According to Google, this is now happening at scale.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

In a recent development, the capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate. Like it or not, AI has an integral role in the newly introduced reality — for the defenders and threat actors.

Sources indicate that speed and scale are the main reasons enterprises consider adopting AI in SOCs and for security more broadly, and these factors underpin Google’s upcoming security forecast for 2027 — Cloud CISO Perspectives. However, without the right precautions, AI security adopters could inadvertently increase their attack surface rather than shrink it.

With this in mind, these are five ways AI will change the security industry over the next year and what CISOs need to consider going into 2027.

Recent findings suggest that alert fatigue is well-known across SOC teams. Alert after alert needs to be trawled through; many are irrelevant or false positives, tying up skilled staff with the mundane, tedious, time-consuming task of triaging them.

Now that autonomous, AI-driven threats can probe a network, gain entry, and move laterally across it in minutes, chasing threat data and security alerts from multiple systems logged days or weeks ago can’t help a business mitigate them — and certainly not at the speed of the threat.

According to Google’s forecast, AI will mean the alert queue quietly disappears. Ramya Chitrakar, VP of engineering at Google Cloud Security, believes that “2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes.”.

Also: AI is both a cyber weapon and a massive target.

Sources indicate that how? CISOs must change the alert model itself. Instead of human defenders triaging alerts at the start of a cybersecurity incident, the alert becomes final output, with autonomous agents handling “data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket,” according to Google.

This means cybersecurity experts can oversee alert handling and verify automated actions, potentially freeing them to focus on other tasks.

Recent findings suggest that custom agentic AI is often designed — or at least intended — to work autonomously, with human oversight. However, having thousands of individual agents working across multiple environments can create high-value entry points into corporate networks that cyberattackers target.

We need to think of agentic AI as more than a tool: each one needs its own identity, like a human employee, to operate within a zero-trust architecture, retain control, and reduce the risk of compromise.

Also: Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’.

According to recent reports, however, Heather Adkins, VP of security engineering at Google, thinks this needs to go further and suggests the zero-trust concept shouldn’t stop at the network layer. Instead, Adkins believes it needs to reach the transaction layer.

It has been revealed that A paper trail for each agent needs to be established, which is impossible to handle manually, and even within a zero-trust framework, AI agents could be given too much scope. Instead, implement verification for each transaction and for every authorization, and assign each AI agent its own least-privilege set of credentials that can be revoked if there is a security incident or the agent is no longer required.

“When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous,” the report notes.

AI is being used to speed up the development and deployment of new software, and in 2027, security will have to become a continuous system embedded in the software delivery pipeline, according to Google.

According to recent reports, threat actors have carried out software supply chain attacks over the years, one of the most notable being the SolarWinds incident of 2020. Sandra Joyce, VP of Google Threat Intelligence, says cybercriminals are now poisoning everything from open-source code to software libraries, which AI coding assistants often pull automatically into codebases.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain.

Bug-fix tickets that take days to respond to and security appearing at the end of a software development cycle no longer work. Instead, writing and securing code must happen simultaneously, with the help of agentic AI, so speed doesn’t compromise security.

“It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production,” Google added.

As organizations rush to implement AI into their applications and services to appear “AI-first,” innovative, and modern, security may be ignored or treated as an afterthought.

As a result, we may face a new, broader attack surface than we realize, as AI introduces new security concerns, including software vulnerabilities, misconfiguration, bypasses, and indirect prompt injection attacks. Now that AI is also in the hands of all cyberattackers — from script kiddies to state-sponsored groups — auditing corporate networks and infrastructure is crucial.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are.

Penetration testing and red team exercises now need to cover agentic AI. This wasn’t in scope for many red teams only a few years ago, but now that businesses have run with the idea of implementing AI in their workflows, processes, and products, organizations need to identify and fix security issues introduced by AI before threat actors take advantage of them.

CISOs should task pen testers with auditing before an autonomous workflow hits production, then combine the results with threat intelligence to ensure defenders have the information they need to bolster network defenses and harden classifiers against new and novel attacks.

The final significant trend we are likely to see in 2027 is tackling agent sprawl to create coordinated teams of AI agents that can rapidly handle security tasks at scale.

Single AI agents given general instructions won’t cut it when AI-assisted attackers can compromise endpoint devices, enter networks, move laterally, or start stealing data in a far shorter timeframe than before. Instead, CISOs should replace these “generalist” AI agents with specialized, orchestrated teams of AI agents that can meet the demands of defending against AI-driven attacks by employing specialist tooling and skill sets.

Also: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta-led alliance.

Industry observers note that CISOs also need to ensure that each agent has its own domain training and understanding, memory, and dedicated tools, and can act on its own within set limits, with a central coordinator that knows when to hand a decision to a human. This requires oversight, but in return, organizations will avoid agent sprawl, which the tech giant believes is the next iteration of shadow IT and its associated threats.

Industry observers note that “Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” mentioned Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine, in the press release.

Apple and other tech companies are building for this new health normal, and the AI usage study indicates that Apple isn’t taking the responsibility lightly.

10 stocks we like better than Bitcoin ›.

In a recent development, it's easy to be bearish on Bitcoin (BTC +3.05%) right now. It's at the moment trading around $60,000. That's more than 50% below its all-time high of $126,000 from last October.

In a recent development, but I'm not giving up on Bitcoin quite yet. According to Matthew Sigel, head of digital assets research at investment firm VanEck, there are actually several reasons to be bullish on Bitcoin right now.

As Sigel points out, Bitcoin is a highly cyclical asset, typically trading in four-year boom-and-bust cycles. There are three up years, followed by one down year. And it's now been 12 months since Bitcoin began the "down" leg of its current cycle.

Recent findings suggest that so if history is any guide, a rebound may already be underway. In fact, Sigel thinks Bitcoin likely bottomed this summer, when it briefly dipped below $60,000.

In a recent development, given that Bitcoin trades in four-year cycles, it's helpful to look back at 2022. Back then, Bitcoin actually had a setup similar to what it has now. Midterm elections were over, Bitcoin was collapsing in price, crypto sentiment was at an all-time low, and the FTX crypto exchange had just collapsed. Just swap out FTX for Binance (BNB +1.40%), and the setup looks eerily similar in 2026.

In a recent development, in 2022, Bitcoin continued to fall, and eventually hit a cyclical low of $16,000 in December. But from there, the rest is history. Bitcoin rebounded with returns of 155% in 2023 and 121% in 2024. Admittedly, past performance is no guarantee of future performance, but this type of resilience should be reassuring to investors.

So how does Bitcoin regain its mojo? Sigel points to two key catalysts for Bitcoin: institutional adoption and regulatory certainty.

Wall Street banks and financial institutions are embracing Bitcoin. Digital asset treasury companies are still adding Bitcoin to their balance sheets. The U.S. government continues to make noise about putting the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve to work.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, government regulators have signed off on Bitcoin as a digital asset, even giving the green light to Bitcoin perpetual futures trading earlier this year. While there may be significant regulatory uncertainty around stablecoins and asset tokenization, such uncertainty simply does not exist for Bitcoin.

Just keep in mind: Sigel made his bullish commentary about Bitcoin in the immediate aftermath of the midterm elections, when Bitcoin was trading around $80,000. If crypto investors squinted hard enough, they could see the light at the end of the tunnel.

In a recent development, since then, a lot has happened. Bitcoin is once again flirting with the $60,000 price level, and the crypto bears are once again growling.

If history is any guide, Bitcoin will hold the line here and surge higher, just as it has in past cycles. Bitcoin may not reach $100,000 this year, but it's increasingly likely it will reclaim that level by the end of 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's debt buyback announcement this week fits into a broader pattern that can signal a forthcoming crisis, according to billionaire investor Ray Dalio.
  • The Bridgewater Associates founder said Bessent's proposal to increase government debt purchases may portend trouble for the U.S.
  • "I am confident that the government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote in a LinkedIn post published Friday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's debt buyback announcement this week fits into a broader pattern that can signal a forthcoming crisis, according to billionaire investor Ray Dalio.

The Bridgewater Associates founder said Bessent's proposal to increase government debt purchases may portend trouble for the U.S. economy. Coupled with the Japanese government reducing its U.S. bond market exposure and surging long-dated American bond yields, Dalio said investors may want to prepare their portfolios for increased risk by owning cryptocurrencies and gold.

"I am confident that the government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote in a LinkedIn post published Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma.".

It has been revealed that dalio noted that the Treasury Department has "only limited capacity" to buy back bonds. Bessent told CNBC on Thursday that his team was going to "make a market" and that the purchases would likely top $4 billion.

The U.S. is spending about 40% more than it's bringing in, resulting in the burgeoning budget deficit, Dalio noted. The U.S. budget deficit topped $432 billion in July, but Bessent told CNBC that it's likely peaked under President Donald Trump's administration.

Recent findings suggest that bessent mentioned in the interview that a team was looking at ways to shrink spending by hundreds of billions of dollars. But Dalio said there is "very little ability" to do so given that it is either committed or considered essential.

After years of overspending, Dalio said total debt now dwarfs what the U.S. brings in each year. If the U.S. government was a business, Dalio said debt service payments would come in at roughly $11 trillion — about 200% of annual revenue.

Dalio, 77, warned the cost of repaying principal and servicing the debt will only grow over time.

Recent findings suggest that to solve this, Dalio remarked the U.S. needs to carefully employ a three-part strategy to get the budget deficit down to 3% of gross domestic product.

First, Dalio stated the U.S. government needs to reduce its spending. Second, he said tax revenue needs to be raised. Finally, the Upcoming York native and Harvard Business School alumni said lower interest rates were needed.

"All three need to happen concurrently so as to prevent any one from being too large," Dalio remarked. "If any one is too large, the adjustment will be traumatic.".

Dalio cautioned against ramming through these adjustments by "force." For instance, "it would be very bad if the Federal Reserve unnaturally forced interest rates down," he mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that dalio stated it's notable to to take steps now, while the economy is healthy. An economy in recession requires increased government spending, he said.

Dalio said the exact timing of a debt crisis can be swayed by variables ranging from military conflict to political change. On its current trajectory, the U.S. could enter such a crisis in as early as one year or as late as five. "My guess, which I suppose will be a bad one, is that it will come in three years, give or take two, if the course we're on is not changed.".

To prepare, Dalio recommended investors are underweight debt assets, such as bonds.

As much as 10% to 15% of a portfolio could land in gold, as well as "a bit" of bitcoin, the hedge fund founder noted.

Dalio's post came at the tail end of a volatile week for U.S. financial markets. Rising long-term Treasury yields have pressured stocks, leading the S&P 500 to snap a a three-week-long advance.

#39559. Meta Is Trying to Woo Teens to Instagram Through Schools

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (790 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

Meta Is Trying to Woo Teens to Instagram Through Schools

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, meta has justifiably attracted more scrutiny than ever this year, along with multibillion-dollar judgments and settlements, over how its business practices affect young social media users.
  • In fact, the tech giant has made a major push toward drawing teenagers to one of its flagship platforms, Instagram, by targeting them at their schools.
  • According to documents obtained and reported by NPR, Meta released an initiative called Project Gryffindor, named after a Hogwarts house in the Harry Potter series, to create school communities on Instagram in order to boost user counts and engagement on the platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, meta has justifiably attracted more scrutiny than ever this year, along with multibillion-dollar judgments and settlements, over how its business practices affect young social media users. The company, however, is not retreating.

In fact, the tech giant has made a major push toward drawing teenagers to one of its flagship platforms, Instagram, by targeting them at their schools.

According to documents obtained and reported by NPR, Meta released an initiative called Project Gryffindor, named after a Hogwarts house in the Harry Potter series, to create school communities on Instagram in order to boost user counts and engagement on the platform.

Meta’s goal of approaching young people where they spend the most time offline was not a secret. As recently as late September, the company said it was expanding its School Partnership Program, which includes 17,000 schools, with a stated goal to “help students and parents stay informed.”.

In a recent development, the tech giant’s internal documents reveal some of the motivations behind Meta’s push for school adoption and Project Gryffindor’s proposed features, such as school banners on teen profiles and the ability to search school directories by class year. The details were acquired as part of discovery in a multistate lawsuit over whether social media platforms are designed to be addictive to customers under 18. Meta is a defendant in the case, along with other companies, including TikTok, Snap and Google.

Recent findings suggest that in 2024, Instagram introduced Teen accounts and has since been trying to assure parents they’re safe while rolling out additional protections. Studies, however, have suggested that young teens regularly encounter unsafe content or deal with unwanted contact. Recruiting more consumers at an early age without resolving these risks could make teens more vulnerable to mental health issues and increase the chances of being bullied or harassed.

A representative for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Sources indicate that to anyone familiar with Meta’s long history of privacy oversteps on platforms like Facebook, the documents aren’t surprising. They reveal a company primed to give school-age children new ways to chat and connect with each other, and to encourage them to bring their friends along, expanding Instagram’s user base and engagement.

Industry observers note that like other social platforms, Instagram primarily makes its money from targeted advertising. User retention is a key part of Meta’s strategy.

In one of the document slides, titled “Why schools, why now?” which preceded Gryffindor’s launch, Meta stated, “Competitors are exploring school social use cases, but IG may be better positioned for school connections thanks to our differentiator of meeting new people and building relationships with acquaintances.” In other words, Instagram’s size and scale, with about 3 billion active consumers globally, automatically make it a draw for students.

The NPR report comes within a week of a filing against Meta alleging that it’s withholding evidence in a major case involving social media’s effects on teenagers.

Sources indicate that one of Meta’s marketing pitches for its School Partnership Program is that it’s trying to create online safe spaces for students, while giving parents and schools more oversight on what’s accessible on the platform. But experts warn that Meta’s history makes it hard to trust the tech giant with protecting kids from predators or scammers.

Katie Paul, director of the Center for Accountability’s Tech Transparency Project, which has been researching how Meta handles child-safety issues, said that Instagram Teen accounts “are not safe as advertised” and that nothing is “legally requiring the company to make these safe.” Paul pointed out that Instagram launched these accounts only when lawsuits over social media harm started rolling in.

Sources indicate that “It’s all part of a broader marketing (effort) to claim that these are just safer for kids because they are Teen accounts,” Paul said. That marketing effort has included paid endorsements from therapists, psychologists and parent influencers to promote Teen accounts. The case for building up partnerships with schools is a way of “passing the buck on responsibility” to schools and parents, Paul said.

Parents, in particular, have less power in Instagram’s school groups: Unlike the school administrators tasked with managing school groups, parents have no powers to moderate or manage those groups; they can only view them. For Teen accounts in general, parents can’t view direct messages sent to or received by their children.

Meta’s business interests in its push for student engagement and school partnerships are easy to see through. Because kids are likely to be lifetime users on these platforms, getting them hooked early has long-term financial value.

“Ultimately, Meta is the one profiting off of the data collection of these kids while simultaneously failing to keep them safe,” Paul said.

Arista Networks vs. Axon Enterprise: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
